extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical mathematics and geometry; readers of Archimedes' treatises
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, lemmas, and propositions from Archimedes on centres of gravity for planar figures (triangles, trapezia, parabolic segments) plus the assumptions and numeration scheme used in The Sand‑Reckoner. Includes constructive/ratio formulas and supporting lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity on median (triangle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity lies on the straight line joining any angle to the middle point of the opposite side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes gives a constructive proof: bisect the opposite side, draw parallels, form parallelograms and small triangles, use properties of centres of gravity for those pieces (Props. 8, 9) to deduce the triangle's centre lies on the median; alternative proof via similarity and decomposition into equal triangles and a parallelogram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection characterization of triangle's centre of gravity (Prop. 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of any triangle is at the intersection of the lines drawn from any two angles to the middle points of the opposite sides respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows immediately from the median result: any two medians meet at the triangle's centre of gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a trapezium (Prop. 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: For trapezium ABCD with AD, BC parallel and AD the smaller, and EF the segment joining midpoints of AD, BC, the centre of gravity G lies on EF such that GE:GF = (2BC + AD) : (2AD + BC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by producing BA and CD to meet at O; using centres of gravity of triangles OAD and OBC (Prop. 13) and decomposing the trapezium into triangles and parallelograms; construct lines dividing BD into three equal parts and draw parallels to find auxiliary centres H, K and intersection G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite parabolic segments centre (Book II, Prop. 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P, P' are two parabolic segments with centres D, E respectively, the centre of gravity of the two segments taken together lies at a point C on DE determined by the relation P : P' = CE : ED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes reduces each segment to an equal-area rectangle placed on corresponding bases so their centres coincide with D, E; then uses proportionality of areas to locate the composite centre on the line DE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: 'inscribed in the recognised manner' (lemma/definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A figure in a parabolic segment is 'inscribed in the recognised manner' by repeatedly inscribing in each remaining parabolic segment a triangle with the same base and height, iterating into the residual segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three immediate properties are recorded: (1) lines joining nearest angles to the vertex are parallel to the base; (2) those lines are bisected by the diameter of the segment; (3) the intercepts on the diameter follow the proportions of successive odd numbers (1,3,5,...). Archimedes indicates these will be proved in order but also shows how they follow from results in Quadrature of the Parabola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of inscribed figure lies on diameter (Prop. 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a figure is inscribed in the recognised manner in a parabolic segment, the centre of gravity of that inscribed figure lies on the diameter of the segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: decompose the inscribed figure into trapezia and a triangle whose individual centres lie on the diameter; hence the whole's centre lies on the diameter by additive properties (Prop. 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional division of diameters for similar inscribed figures (Prop. 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two similar parabolic segments have diameters AO, ao and analogous figures inscribed in the recognised manner (same number of sides), the centres of gravity of the inscribed figures divide AO and ao in the same ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the lemma that the diameters are cut in segments proportional to 1:3:5:7... and shows corresponding trapezia and triangles are in proportion, so their centres divide AO and ao correspondingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity of a parabolic segment lies on its diameter (Prop. 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of gravity of any parabolic segment cut off by a straight line lies on the diameter of that segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument by contradiction: inscribe a recognised-figure whose centre lies on the diameter (Prop. 2), compare areas so that remainder's centre would have to lie on a line causing all remaining pieces to be on one side — impossible by earlier postulate; hence centre must lie on the diameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment's centre nearer vertex than inscribed figure's centre (Prop. 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a parabolic segment, the centre of gravity of the whole segment is nearer to the vertex than the centre of gravity of any figure inscribed in the recognised manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by constructing triangle with centre F (at AF:FO = 2:1) and demonstrating via decomposition and proportionality that the segment's centre G lies between the midpoints of centres of equal subsegments and F, hence closer to the vertex than F; extend inductively to general inscribed figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation of centres by inscribed figures (Prop. 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a parabolic segment and any assigned length D, one can inscribe a figure (in the recognised manner) so that the distance between the centre of gravity of the segment and that of the inscribed figure is less than D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an inscribed figure leaving total leftover area less than a bound S so that ratios force the remainder's centre to lie within any preassigned distance by contradiction (if not, impossible because remaining pieces lie on one side of a suitable line).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-ratio division for centres of similar segments (Prop. 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two similar parabolic segments have diameters AO, ao and centres G, g, then G and g divide AO and ao respectively in the same ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume different ratio, inscribe close-approximating figures to derive impossibility via previous propositions (esp. Prop. 6 and proportionality results). Archimedes notes the proposition holds more generally than just similar segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical relation for centre of parabolic segment: AG = 3·GO (Prop. 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabolic segment with diameter AO and centre of gravity G, AG = 3 · GO (i.e. AG:GO = 3:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses decomposition into triangle and two equal subsegments, application of Prop. 7 to proportional divisions, and a chain of lemmas and proportional equalities (including results from Quadrature of the Parabola) to compute ratios between centres of component pieces and deduce AG = 3 GO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic lemma on continued proportion (Prop. 9, lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a, b, c, d are four lines in continued proportion and descending order and certain algebraic relations (given in text) hold, then a derived variable y equals 2a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes presents a geometrical proof translatable into algebra; the lemma supports ratio manipulations needed in subsequent Proposition 10. The printed proof carries out substitutions and cross-multiplications to deduce y = 2a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity for area between parallel chords of parabola (Prop. 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a portion of a parabola intercepted between two parallel chords PP', BB' with diametral bisectors N,O and NO divided into five equal parts (middle LM), a point G on LM with LG:GM = BO·(2PN+BO) : PN·(2BO+PN) is the centre of gravity of area PP'B'B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs an auxiliary homologous configuration on a model diameter ao with proportional segments in continued proportion; uses Prop. 9 lemma and Prop. 8 to relate centres of component segments and show G has the required proportional property, then deduces G is the composite centre by area ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption on Earth's perimeter (Sand‑Reckoner, Assumption 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the perimeter of the earth is about 3,000,000 stadia and not greater (Archimedes adopts a conservative upper bound compared with some predecessors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a working numerical upper bound for later large-number estimates; Archimedes notes others had given smaller values but he takes ten times a predecessor's estimate to be safe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative diameters of Earth, Moon, Sun (Sand‑Reckoner, Assumption 2 & 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the diameter of the earth is greater than the moon's, and the diameter of the sun is greater than the earth's; specifically assume the sun's diameter is about 30 times the moon's and not greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes notes alternative earlier astronomical estimates (9x, 12x, ~18–20x) but chooses 30x to ensure upper bounds in his estimates are indisputable; these assumptions feed into geometric chord/arc comparisons used to bound sizes in the following argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption comparing sun with chiliagon side (Sand‑Reckoner, Assumption 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the diameter of the sun is greater than the side of a chiliagon (1000‑gon) inscribed in the greatest circle of the 'universe' (as defined by astronomers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes uses this (provable by an experimental estimation of the sun's angular size) to relate the sun’s diameter to an inscribed polygonal side, which in turn bounds the universe's diameter in stadia via polygon perimeters and earlier perimeter assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption on grain/poppy‑seed size (Sand‑Reckoner, Assumption 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a quantity of sand not greater than a poppy‑seed contains at most 10,000 grains, and that the poppy‑seed diameter is at least 1/4 of a finger‑breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conservative (upper) estimate of grain density is used to derive lower/upper bounds on the total number of grains of sand in large volumes constructed from the earth/universe dimensions; Archimedes makes explicit such practical assumptions to make his enumeration concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeration scheme for very large numbers (orders and periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic naming scheme: numbers up to 10,000 (a myriad) form orders, groups of (100,000,000) constitute higher orders, and these orders are arranged into periods; proceed iteratively to define units of successive orders and periods up to extremely large numbers (denoted P, P', P^*, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes defines 'first period' (orders up to 10^8), then constructs second and further periods by taking P (10^8 orders) as new unit, repeating to reach astronomically large named magnitudes; used to express counts vastly exceeding conventional naming systems of his time.
